title: Field Notes from a Skeptic Who Stayed
script: Narrator: [contemplative] Field notes, three in the morning, because insomnia has apparently become my preferred venue for theology these days.
Narrator: [wry] I spent a decade training myself to distrust any claim that couldn't survive a peer review process, and tauhid, admittedly, doesn't submit to journals.
Narrator: [honestly] What kept me tethered wasn't a syllogism that finally silenced my objections. It was noticing how conveniently my doubt arrived whenever obedience grew inconvenient.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I'd dressed inconvenience up as intellectual rigor for years, congratulating myself on a skepticism that was, on closer inspection, remarkably selective.
Narrator: [reflective] The turning point wasn't a debate I won. It was a debate I finally admitted I'd been quietly rigging from the outset.
Narrator: [wry] Colleagues assume faith and empiricism sit in permanent opposition, as though certainty about causation were something physics itself actually offers anyone.
Narrator: [thoughtful] It doesn't, not really. Every experiment I run rests on assumptions I cannot ultimately prove, only trust provisionally, the way I now trust considerably larger claims.
Narrator: [honestly] That's not a knockdown argument for tauhid, I want to be careful here. It's simply an admission that my prior certainty was borrowed, not earned.
Narrator: [reflective] What tauhid asked of me wasn't the abandonment of inquiry, but the humility to admit inquiry has a ceiling I kept mistaking for a wall.
Narrator: [gently] Behind that ceiling, I've started to suspect, isn't absence at all. It's simply a vantage point mine was never built to reach unaided.
Narrator: [thoughtful] My mother, who never finished secondary school, arrived at conclusions it took me a doctorate and considerable stubbornness to approach sideways.
Narrator: [wry] I used to find that humbling in an uncomfortable way. Now I mostly just find it funny, in the way true things often are.
Narrator: [determined] Tomorrow I'll run the same experiments, cite the same rigorous standards, distrust the same shoddy methodology I've always distrusted on principle.
Narrator: [peacefully] But I'll do it, finally, as someone who suspects the universe was authored rather than merely occurring, and finds that suspicion oddly steadying.
Narrator: [warmly] Field notes end here. Whoever reads these eventually, know that certainty came slower than I expected, and considerably gentler than I feared.

quiz.question: What does the narrator identify as the actual turning point in his belief?
options: Winning a formal debate
Admitting he'd been rigging his own doubt whenever obedience grew inconvenient
Reading a religious text for the first time
A conversation with a colleague
quiz.explanation: He says the turning point wasn't a debate he won, but admitting his doubt conveniently arrived whenever obedience was inconvenient.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say about his prior skepticism upon reflection?
options: It was purely rational and consistent
It was remarkably selective, dressed up as intellectual rigor
It never actually existed
It was shared by all his colleagues equally
quiz.explanation: He admits his skepticism was 'remarkably selective' rather than the consistent rigor he'd credited himself with.

quiz.question: What comparison does the narrator draw between scientific experiments and faith?
options: They have nothing in common
Experiments rest on unprovable assumptions trusted provisionally, similar to larger claims he now trusts
Experiments are more reliable than any belief
Faith requires no trust at all
quiz.explanation: He notes that every experiment rests on assumptions he cannot ultimately prove, only trust provisionally, paralleling his trust in larger claims.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say tauhid actually asked of him?
options: To abandon all inquiry and questioning
To admit inquiry has a ceiling he'd mistaken for a wall
To stop working as a researcher
To reject scientific methodology entirely
quiz.explanation: He states tauhid didn't demand abandoning inquiry, only humility about inquiry's ceiling, which he'd mistaken for an impassable wall.

quiz.question: How does the narrator describe his mother's understanding compared to his own?
options: She understood far less than he did
She arrived at conclusions it took him a doctorate and stubbornness to approach sideways
She never discussed belief with him
Her education exceeded his own
quiz.explanation: He notes his mother, without formal education, reached conclusions that took him a doctorate and considerable stubbornness to approach.

title: A Late-Night Broadcast on Whether Meaning Requires an Author
script: Host: [warmly] It's late, but insomniac listeners deserve serious company, so tonight we're tackling a question our inbox keeps returning to. Professor Hakim, welcome back.
Guest: [pleasantly] Always glad to keep strange hours for good questions.
Host: [curious] Someone wrote asking why an all-wise God would permit suffering that appears, by any reasonable measure, entirely gratuitous.
Guest: [thoughtful] Gratuitous is doing a great deal of work in that sentence. It assumes we're positioned to judge which suffering serves a purpose and which doesn't.
Host: [pressing] Isn't that a convenient assumption for someone defending divine wisdom, though? Unfalsifiable, essentially.
Guest: [amused] Fair challenge. But unfalsifiable isn't synonymous with false, it simply means the claim operates outside empirical adjudication entirely.
Host: [thoughtful] So where does that leave someone who wants intellectual honesty rather than comfortable evasion?
Guest: [reflective] Exactly where every serious epistemic question eventually leaves us, choosing which uncertainty we're actually willing to live inside.
Host: [curious] Meaning what, practically speaking?
Guest: [gently] Meaning atheism doesn't escape the problem, it just relocates it. Suffering without any author is arguably harder to metabolize than suffering with an inscrutable one.
Host: [interested] That's a subtler point than I expected tonight.
Guest: [warmly] Most genuine points are subtler than expected, that's rather the trouble with genuine points.
Host: [thoughtful] Some listeners will hear inscrutable wisdom and simply think that's another word for indifference.
Guest: [firm] I'd resist that translation. Inscrutability describes the limits of our vantage point, not the character of the wisdom itself.
Host: [curious] How do you hold that distinction without it curdling into denial of real pain?
Guest: [honestly] Carefully, and imperfectly, most days. I don't think theology was ever meant to anesthetize grief, only to keep it from metastasizing into despair.
Host: [thoughtful] That distinction, grief without despair, feels like the actual thesis of tonight's conversation.
Guest: [warmly] It rather is. Despair assumes the story has already ended. Grief simply admits this particular chapter is unbearable.
Host: [smiling] On that note, we'll let our night owls sit with something harder than easy comfort tonight.
Guest: [warmly] As they should. Comfort arrives eventually, on its own schedule. Honesty has to arrive first, always.

quiz.question: What does the guest say the word 'gratuitous' assumes when applied to suffering?
options: That all suffering is equally distributed
That we're positioned to judge which suffering serves a purpose and which doesn't
That suffering never has any cause
That gratuitous suffering is common knowledge
quiz.explanation: The guest says calling suffering gratuitous assumes we can judge which suffering serves a purpose, a judgment we may not be positioned to make.

quiz.question: How does the guest respond to the charge that his position is unfalsifiable?
options: He denies the charge entirely
He agrees unfalsifiable isn't the same as false, only outside empirical adjudication
He says unfalsifiable claims are always true
He refuses to answer the question
quiz.explanation: He concedes the claim is unfalsifiable but clarifies that unfalsifiable is not synonymous with false.

quiz.question: What does the guest argue about atheism and the problem of suffering?
options: Atheism fully solves the problem of suffering
Atheism relocates rather than escapes the problem, since authorless suffering may be harder to metabolize
Atheism has nothing to say about suffering
Suffering only exists within religious frameworks
quiz.explanation: The guest argues atheism doesn't escape the problem of suffering, it relocates it, since suffering without any author may be harder to bear.

quiz.question: What distinction does the guest draw regarding 'inscrutable wisdom'?
options: It is identical to indifference
Inscrutability describes the limits of human vantage point, not the character of the wisdom itself
It only applies to modern problems
It proves wisdom does not exist
quiz.explanation: He resists equating inscrutability with indifference, saying it describes our limited vantage point rather than the nature of the wisdom.

quiz.question: What does the guest identify as the actual thesis of the conversation?
options: That grief should be avoided entirely
Grief without despair, since despair assumes the story has ended while grief admits only the current chapter is unbearable
That comfort must arrive before honesty
That theology should anesthetize all pain
quiz.explanation: The guest affirms grief without despair as the thesis, distinguishing despair, which assumes the story has ended, from grief, which admits only this chapter is unbearable.

title: Two Analysts Argue About Whether Ambition Is a Form of Distrust
script: Nadia: [needling] Farid, you turned down the promotion. Again. I need you to justify that to me like I'm a shareholder.
Farid: [amused] I'm not required to justify contentment to anyone, least of all a shareholder who works ninety-hour weeks.
Nadia: [firm] It's not contentment, it's abdication dressed up in spiritual vocabulary. Tawakkul doesn't mean refusing opportunities that land in your lap.
Farid: [thoughtful] I didn't refuse it out of piety, actually. I refused it because it would have cost me every evening I currently spend with my children.
Nadia: [skeptical] Convenient that piety and convenience aligned so neatly in this particular case.
Farid: [laughing] They don't always, believe me. I've made plenty of decisions where trusting Allah cost me considerably more than a corner office.
Nadia: [pressing] Name one, then.
Farid: [honestly] I turned down a client whose contract required cutting ethical corners I wasn't willing to cut, knowing it would tighten our budget for a year.
Nadia: [quieter] I remember that quarter. I assumed you'd simply miscalculated the market.
Farid: [gently] Everyone assumed that. Nobody assumes trust in providence when the numbers look inconvenient, they assume incompetence instead, quietly.
Nadia: [thoughtful] I suppose ambition is simply easier to read as virtue than restraint ever is.
Farid: [warmly] Considerably easier. Restraint doesn't photograph well on a resume, unfortunately for people like me.
Nadia: [honestly] I think what unsettles me is that I've built my entire identity around never being the one who says no to more.
Farid: [gently] That's worth sitting with, more than my career choices are, frankly speaking.
Nadia: [reflective] Is it exhausting, though, choosing the smaller path deliberately, over and over, year after year?
Farid: [honestly] Some weeks, enormously so. I don't romanticize it. I just no longer mistake exhaustion for evidence that I chose wrongly.
Nadia: [softly] I don't know if I could tell the difference between distrust and discipline in my own decisions anymore.
Farid: [warmly] Start by asking what you're actually afraid would happen if you said no once. That usually clarifies things quickly.
Nadia: [wry] I'm afraid nothing would happen, and I'd have to admit the striving was never really about provision at all.
Farid: [gently] Now that, Nadia, is a considerably more honest answer than the shareholder speech you opened with.

quiz.question: Why did Farid actually turn down the promotion, according to him?
options: He was not qualified for it
It would have cost him every evening he spends with his children
His company was struggling financially
He disliked his manager
quiz.explanation: Farid explains he refused the promotion because it would have cost him time with his children, not out of piety alone.

quiz.question: What example does Farid give of a decision where trust in Allah cost him more than convenience?
options: Selling his house
Turning down a client whose contract required cutting ethical corners, tightening his budget for a year
Quitting his job entirely
Moving to another city
quiz.explanation: Farid describes refusing a client's unethical contract terms, which tightened his budget for a year.

quiz.question: How did people interpret Farid's decision at the time, according to him?
options: They assumed trust in providence
They assumed incompetence rather than trust in providence
They praised his ethics publicly
They ignored the decision completely
quiz.explanation: Farid notes that nobody assumed trust in providence when the numbers looked inconvenient; they quietly assumed incompetence instead.

quiz.question: What does Nadia admit unsettles her about her own identity?
options: She fears being seen as lazy
She has built her identity around never saying no to more
She dislikes her current job entirely
She regrets her education
quiz.explanation: Nadia admits she has built her entire identity around never being the one who says no to more opportunity.

quiz.question: What does Nadia ultimately fear would happen if she said no once?
options: She would lose her job immediately
Nothing would happen, forcing her to admit her striving was never really about provision
Her colleagues would replace her
She would become instantly content
quiz.explanation: Nadia admits she fears nothing would happen, meaning she'd have to acknowledge her striving was never truly about provision.

title: On Teaching My Daughter to Doubt Well
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] My daughter, sixteen now, came to me last month and announced, with the particular gravity only teenagers manage, that she wasn't sure she believed in anything anymore.
Narrator: [honestly] My first instinct was panic, dressed up as calm. My second instinct, thankfully, arrived a few seconds later and was considerably wiser than the first.
Narrator: [reflective] I remembered my own adolescence, the quiet doubts I never voiced, because voicing them felt like betrayal rather than the ordinary business of growing a mind.
Narrator: [gently] So instead of arguments, I asked what specifically felt uncertain, expecting theology and receiving, instead, something closer to grief about suffering she'd witnessed firsthand.
Narrator: [thoughtful] She'd watched a classmate's family lose everything in a flood, and no explanation I could offer would have satisfied the question underneath her question.
Narrator: [honestly] I told her I didn't have a tidy answer, and watched something in her posture relax, as though permission to not know had been the actual request.

Narrator: [reflective] We talked instead about the difference between doubting Allah's existence and doubting our own capacity to fully grasp His wisdom, a distinction I wish someone had offered me earlier.
Narrator: [warmly] I told her real faith isn't the absence of hard questions, it's choosing to keep asking them honestly rather than either suppressing or abandoning them entirely.
Narrator: [thoughtful] She asked whether I still had questions like hers, and I admitted, yes, plenty, some I've carried for twenty years without resolution.
Narrator: [gently] That admission seemed to steady her more than any answer could have, which taught me something about what teenagers actually need from us.
Narrator: [determined] I'm not raising her to inherit my certainties wholesale, that would be intellectually dishonest and, frankly, a little cowardly on my part.
Narrator: [warmly] I'm raising her to doubt rigorously, question sincerely, and land, eventually, wherever honest inquiry actually takes her, even if that path winds longer than mine did.
Narrator: [reflective] Some nights I worry that's a risk. Other nights I suspect it's the only form of faith sturdy enough to survive an entire lifetime intact.
Narrator: [peacefully] She still isn't certain of everything. Neither am I, honestly, and I've finally stopped pretending that uncertainty disqualifies either of us from belief.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's daughter announce to her last month?
options: That she wanted to change schools
That she wasn't sure she believed in anything anymore
That she wanted to move out
That she had failed an exam
quiz.explanation: The daughter announced, with teenage gravity, that she wasn't sure she believed in anything anymore.

quiz.question: What was actually underneath the daughter's doubt, once the narrator asked?
options: Boredom with religious classes
Grief about suffering she'd witnessed after a classmate's family lost everything in a flood
Disagreement with a teacher
Peer pressure from friends
quiz.explanation: The daughter's doubt stemmed from grief over witnessing a classmate's family lose everything in a flood.

quiz.question: What distinction did the narrator introduce to her daughter?
options: The difference between prayer and fasting
The difference between doubting Allah's existence and doubting our capacity to grasp His wisdom
The difference between science and religion
The difference between hope and fear
quiz.explanation: The narrator distinguished doubting Allah's existence from doubting our own limited capacity to fully grasp His wisdom.

quiz.question: What did the narrator admit when her daughter asked if she still had similar questions?
options: That she had never doubted anything
That she had plenty of unresolved questions carried for twenty years
That doubt was forbidden
That she stopped believing entirely
quiz.explanation: The narrator admitted she still carries plenty of unresolved questions, some for twenty years.

quiz.question: What kind of faith does the narrator say she hopes to raise her daughter toward?
options: Faith built on inherited certainty without question
Rigorous, sincere questioning that lands wherever honest inquiry leads, even if it takes longer
Faith that avoids all doubt entirely
Faith identical to her own in every detail
quiz.explanation: She says she is raising her daughter to doubt rigorously and question sincerely, landing wherever honest inquiry leads, even on a longer path.

title: Siblings Debate the Job Offer in Doha
script: Yasmin: [anxious] Reza, if I take this position, I'm choosing to be four time zones from Mom for three years.
Reza: [thoughtful] I know. I've been running the same calculation since you told me, and still don't have a clean answer.
Yasmin: [frustrated] Everyone keeps saying trust Allah's plan, as though that phrase resolves the actual logistics of who takes Mom to appointments.
Reza: [gently] It doesn't resolve logistics, you're right. I think it's meant to resolve something else, the part of you convinced this decision determines everything permanently.
Yasmin: [honestly] Doesn't it, though? If something happens while I'm overseas, I don't think I'd forgive myself, regardless of what theology says about qadar.
Reza: [firm] I'd be here. That's not a small variable in this equation, even if it's easy to discount your own presence when leaving.
Yasmin: [softly] I know. I think that's actually part of my guilt, leaving you to carry what should be shared.
Reza: [warmly] Then let's share it, instead of you carrying preemptive guilt for a decision you haven't even made yet.
Reza: [reflective] Weekly calls with her doctor, splitting costs evenly, and you flying back for anything serious, no negotiation there.
Yasmin: [considering] That sounds manageable, said out loud, rather than the catastrophe I've been rehearsing at two in the morning.
Reza: [gently] Most catastrophes sound manageable once someone else calmly says them back to you.
Yasmin: [honestly] I think what I need permission for isn't the job, it's wanting something for myself while Mom needs more from us.
Reza: [warmly] You have that, from me at least. Provision was never meant to require shrinking your entire life around one variable.
Yasmin: [reflective] I keep forgetting tawakkul includes trusting Allah with the people I love, not only with my own outcomes.
Reza: [gently] Exactly that. You're not abandoning her by trusting she remains held even in your absence.
Yasmin: [determined] Okay. I'll accept it, then, and we build the logistics properly instead of quietly panicking alone.
Reza: [warmly] Good. Call her more than the calendar requires. Guilt shrinks considerably when you're actually present, even long-distance.
Yasmin: [softly] I will. Thank you for not just telling me what I wanted to hear.
Reza: [warmly] That's not what siblings are for. Go accept the job before you talk yourself out of it.

quiz.question: What is Yasmin deciding about in this conversation?
options: Whether to get married
Whether to accept a job offer in Doha that would keep her far from their mother
Whether to buy a house
Whether to change careers entirely
quiz.explanation: Yasmin is deciding whether to accept a job in Doha, which would put her four time zones from their mother for years.

quiz.question: What does Yasmin say frustrates her about the phrase 'trust Allah's plan'?
options: She thinks it is untrue
It doesn't resolve the actual logistics of who takes their mother to appointments
She has never heard the phrase before
It only applies to financial decisions
quiz.explanation: Yasmin is frustrated that the phrase doesn't address the practical logistics of caregiving.

quiz.question: What practical plan does Reza propose for sharing responsibility?
options: Yasmin should decline the job entirely
Weekly doctor calls, splitting costs evenly, and Yasmin flying back for anything serious
Hiring a full-time caregiver only
Moving their mother to Doha
quiz.explanation: Reza proposes weekly calls with the doctor, evenly split costs, and Yasmin flying back for serious matters.

quiz.question: What does Yasmin realize she actually needs permission for?
options: Permission to quit working entirely
Wanting something for herself while her mother needs more from them
Permission to stop praying
Permission to ignore her mother's needs
quiz.explanation: Yasmin realizes what she needs permission for is wanting something for herself while her mother has greater needs.

quiz.question: What broader understanding of tawakkul does Yasmin arrive at?
options: That tawakkul only applies to her own outcomes
That tawakkul includes trusting Allah with the people she loves, not only her own outcomes
That tawakkul means avoiding all difficult decisions
That tawakkul requires staying physically close to family always
quiz.explanation: Yasmin realizes tawakkul includes trusting Allah with the people she loves, not solely with her own ambitions and outcomes.

title: On the Grammar of Providence
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] I've noticed something curious about the language for good fortune versus hardship, and it reveals more theology than we intend.
Narrator: [reflective] When something goes well, we say I got the job, active voice, personal agency fully claimed, credit filed under my own name.
Narrator: [honestly] When something goes badly, the grammar shifts instinctively. It happened to me. Suddenly we're passive recipients of a universe conspiring against us.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Tauhid, I've come to think, asks us to notice this grammatical sleight of hand and correct it consistently, in both directions, not just the convenient one.
Narrator: [gently] Everything, the promotion and the diagnosis alike, arrives from the same source, however differently we're inclined to file the paperwork afterward.
Narrator: [reflective] That's not a claim that effort is irrelevant, I want to be precise here, because sloppy theology tends to collapse nuance into slogans rather quickly.
Narrator: [honestly] Effort matters enormously, causation within this world is entirely real, but causation was never the same thing as ultimate authorship, and we conflate them constantly.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I spent years crediting myself lavishly for outcomes I'd actually only partially engineered, then blaming fate exclusively for outcomes I'd partially engineered too.
Narrator: [wry] It's a remarkably self-serving grammar, now that I've noticed it, one that assigns me authorship only when authorship happens to flatter me conveniently.
Narrator: [gently] Correcting it hasn't made me passive, contrary to what I expected. If anything, I plan more carefully now, precisely because I'm no longer terrified of outcomes defining me.
Narrator: [reflective] When the plan succeeds, I say alhamdulillah before I say I did it, and the order of those two sentences has quietly reorganized something inside me.
Narrator: [honestly] When the plan collapses, I try, imperfectly some days, to resist the passive victimhood that grammar so eagerly offers me instead.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Language shapes belief more than we readily admit, and belief, eventually, reshapes language right back, each one training the other over years.
Narrator: [warmly] I'm not fluent yet in this corrected grammar, honestly, I still slip into old tenses under real pressure more often than I'd like to admit.
Narrator: [peacefully] But I notice the slipping now, every time, and noticing, I've found, is precisely where every real correction actually begins.

quiz.question: What grammatical pattern does the narrator notice in how people describe fortune versus hardship?
options: People always use passive voice for everything
Good fortune gets active voice claiming credit, while hardship shifts to passive voice as though happening to us
There is no difference in language used
Hardship is always described in active voice
quiz.explanation: The narrator notices good fortune is described actively, claiming credit, while hardship shifts to passive voice as though it simply happened to the person.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say tauhid asks people to do with this grammatical pattern?
options: Ignore it completely
Notice the sleight of hand and correct it consistently in both directions
Only correct it for hardship, not fortune
Replace all grammar with religious language
quiz.explanation: He says tauhid asks us to notice this pattern and correct it consistently, in both directions, not just when convenient.

quiz.question: What clarification does the narrator make about effort and causation?
options: Effort is irrelevant to outcomes
Effort and causation are real, but causation was never the same thing as ultimate authorship
Causation does not exist in this world
Effort guarantees successful outcomes
quiz.explanation: He clarifies effort matters and causation is real, but causation is not the same as ultimate authorship, which people often conflate.

quiz.question: What has changed in the order of the narrator's response to success?
options: He now says 'I did it' before anything else
He now says alhamdulillah before saying 'I did it'
He no longer acknowledges his own effort
He avoids discussing success altogether
quiz.explanation: He says when a plan succeeds, he now says alhamdulillah before crediting himself, a reordering that reorganized something inside him.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say about his fluency in this 'corrected grammar'?
options: He has mastered it completely
He is not yet fluent and still slips into old patterns under real pressure
He never uses the old grammar anymore
He gave up trying to change it
quiz.explanation: He admits he isn't fluent yet and still slips into old tenses under real pressure, but now notices the slipping.

title: An Evening Broadcast with a Painter Who Stopped Reading Reviews
script: Host: [warmly] Tonight's guest hasn't read a single review of his work in four years, which sounds like either enlightenment or denial, and I intend to find out which.
Guest: [laughing] Possibly both, depending on the particular week you happen to catch me.
Host: [curious] Walk us through what changed. Four years ago you were, by your own account, obsessive about critical reception.
Guest: [reflective] Obsessive undersells it. I'd refresh reviews compulsively, and my entire mood hinged on strangers' assessments of work already finished.
Host: [thoughtful] What finally interrupted that particular cycle?
Guest: [honestly] A particularly savage review, oddly enough, one that dismantled a piece I genuinely believed was my best work to date.
Host: [curious] And that broke the habit, rather than intensifying it further?
Guest: [thoughtful] It broke something else first, actually, my quiet assumption that validation was mine to secure through sufficient talent or effort.
Host: [interested] That sounds like a fairly severe crisis for a working artist to weather.
Guest: [honestly] It was. I genuinely considered abandoning the craft entirely for months, which tells you how much authority I'd handed to strangers with keyboards.
Host: [gently] What brought you back to painting, eventually, after all that?
Guest: [warmly] A conversation with an imam, actually, unexpected setting for an artistic crisis, who asked whether I made work for Allah or for applause.
Host: [thoughtful] That's a rather harsh question to sit with.
Guest: [laughing] Extremely harsh, and entirely necessary. I hadn't separated the two in years, maybe ever, if I'm honest about it.
Host: [curious] Has separating them changed the actual work itself, in practice?
Guest: [reflective] Considerably. I take stranger risks now, ones I'd have previously abandoned for fear of alienating an audience I no longer center quite so completely.
Host: [thoughtful] Do you miss the validation, even now, if you're being honest?
Guest: [honestly] Sometimes, sure. I'm not claiming spiritual immunity to the human craving for recognition, that would be entirely dishonest of me.
Host: [gently] What do you do, then, on the days you crave it most?
Guest: [warmly] I remind myself the work was sincere when I made it, and sincerity, unlike applause, doesn't depreciate based on strangers' opinions afterward.
Host: [smiling] That's a rather steadying note to end our broadcast on tonight.
Guest: [warmly] Steadier than reading reviews, certainly. Goodnight, and paint something honest tomorrow.

quiz.question: How long has the guest gone without reading reviews of his work?
options: One year
Four years
Ten years
He has never stopped reading them
quiz.explanation: The host notes the guest hasn't read a single review in four years.

quiz.question: What actually interrupted the guest's compulsive review-checking cycle?
options: A positive review that boosted his confidence
A particularly savage review that dismantled a piece he believed was his best work
His manager forbade him from reading reviews
He simply lost interest in painting
quiz.explanation: A savage review dismantling what he believed was his best work broke the cycle by shattering his assumption about validation.

quiz.question: What assumption did the harsh review break, according to the guest?
options: That painting was a viable career
That validation was his to secure through sufficient talent or effort
That reviews were always accurate
That he needed formal art training
quiz.explanation: The review broke his quiet assumption that validation was something he could secure through enough talent or effort.

quiz.question: What question did the imam ask the guest that proved pivotal?
options: Whether he needed a new agent
Whether he made work for Allah or for applause
Whether he should change his artistic style
Whether he had considered a different career
quiz.explanation: The imam asked whether the guest made his work for Allah or for applause, a question the guest calls harsh but necessary.

quiz.question: What does the guest tell himself on days he still craves validation?
options: That he should quit painting
That the work was sincere when made, and sincerity doesn't depreciate based on others' opinions
That validation no longer matters to anyone
That he should read reviews again to check
quiz.explanation: He reminds himself the work was sincere when made, and unlike applause, sincerity doesn't depreciate based on strangers' opinions.
